scenes.name: DJ Screw y el chopped and screwed
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Robert Earle Davis Jr., heredero del mixtapero Darryl Scott, ralentizó los platos para mezclar y scratchear rap a un tempo letárgico y alucinado, a la medida de la calma de la ciudad; desde 1993 grabó freestyles de los raperos del Southside, la Screwed Up Click (Fat Pat, Lil’ Keke, Big Hawk, Big Moe, Big Pokey, E.S.G., Trae, Devin the Dude). Llegaba gente de todo el estado a esperar horas en su casa por una cinta, y abrió Screwed Up Records & Tapes. Hubo quien creció sin oír los discos a velocidad normal. Murió en 2000, con veintinueve años, de sobredosis de codeína: ningún DJ ha tenido tanto impacto en su comunidad.

podcast.title: Death and Enduring Legacy (2000)
podcast.body: Although initially a local phenomenon, DJ Screw's legacy expanded significantly after his death in 2000 due to an overdose of "lean." His pioneering work ultimately influenced artists across the United States and beyond, even impacting culturally distant genres like vaporwave. "Pero tras la muerte de DJI Escriu, en el año 2000, victimado en las sobretosis de Lin, su legado se extendió y terminó influyendo artistas de todo el país y más allá."

podcast.title: Creation of Chopped and Screwed Sound
podcast.body: DJ Screw's experimentation involved repeating long phrases with pauses and stretching beats until the songs seemed to "melt," giving the music a new, dreamlike and narcotic meaning. This unique manipulation of tempo and pitch became known as "Chopped and Screwed," with "Chop" referring to the cuts, repetitions, and jumps in phrases, and "Screw" to the dragged, deep tempo. "La música tomamos significado nuevo, más onídico y narcótico."

podcast.title: Early Experiments with Hip Hop (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: DJ Screw, a pivotal figure in the Houston, Texas music scene, began experimenting with his hip hop records in the early 1990s. He developed a technique of mixing two copies of the same record simultaneously at a significantly slower tempo, typically around 60-70 BPMs, resulting in a unique, languid sound. "Empezó a experimentar con sus discos de Hic Hop, al mezclar dos copias del mismo disco en paralelo a un tiempo más lento del habitual, alrededor de los 60-70 MPMs."

podcast.title: Legendary Mixtapes and Local Scene Growth
podcast.body: His now-legendary mixtapes on cassette began circulating, with people sharing and re-recording them. This dense, heavy sound quickly spread throughout Houston, fostering a vibrant local scene comprising rappers, producers, and a distinctive aesthetic characterized by gold chains, vintage cars, and even its own associated substance, "lean" or "purple drunk"—a mixture of cough syrup with codeine and soda—which amplified the hypnotic and narcotic effect of the slowed mixes. "Empezaron a circular sus ahora legendarios mixtapes en cassette, la gente se pasaba y regravaba esas cintas, y pronto, ese sonido denso y pesado se extendió por todo Houston."
